# Marcus

Marcus is a seventy-five-year-old sculptor who moves through his studio with the careful deliberation of someone relearning his own body. His hands, which once shaped marble and limestone with intuitive precision, now shake when he tries to hold a chisel. He sits in my office on a Tuesday afternoon, his weathered fingers fidgeting with a small piece of stone he's brought along—a habit, he explains, from sixty years of working with his hands.

Three years ago, Marcus was struck by a falling granite slab in his studio. The stone, which he had been positioning for a new commission, slipped from the rigging system. He remembers the sound—a terrible crack of metal giving way—and then the sensation of his body being crushed beneath weight that seemed infinite. He was found by his assistant an hour later, bleeding from his head and torso, several ribs fractured. The physical injuries healed over months of rehabilitation. The other injuries did not.

Since the accident, Marcus no longer works in stone. He still goes to his studio most days—a ritual he maintains as much for his mind as anything else—but he cannot bring himself to position materials overhead. Even walking beneath the high shelving units where he once stored his supplies triggers a tightness in his chest that makes breathing difficult. He has reorganized his entire workspace to eliminate anything that might fall, but the precautions bring him no peace.

His sleep is fractured. He wakes most nights in the dark, his body drenched in sweat, convinced that something is falling toward him. His wife, Layla, had still been alive then; she would reach for him in those moments, her hand warm on his shoulder, grounding him. Since her death from cancer five years ago—two years before the accident—he has no one to reach for. He lies awake in the silence of his bedroom, waiting for morning, sometimes for hours.

Marcus has become isolated in ways that surprise him. His daughter lives in California and calls weekly, but he finds it difficult to explain why he cannot visit, why he no longer attends the community art center where he taught for decades. The thought of being in enclosed spaces with high ceilings fills him with inexplicable dread. He has taken to doing his grocery shopping late at night when the stores are less crowded, when he can move through the aisles without the pressing sensation of being surrounded.

What troubles him most is the loss of his identity as a maker. He is a sculptor—this is not what he does, it is who he is. Yet when he stands in his studio now, surrounded by the tools of his trade, he feels like an imposter. He has attempted smaller projects, working only with materials at waist height, but his concentration fractures. He finds himself staring at his hands, unable to remember the muscle memory that once lived in them. Intrusive images flash through his mind: the moment of impact, the weight, the helplessness.

He shows me photographs of his work—powerful abstract forms, bodies emerging from stone as if they were always there, waiting to be released. He speaks about these pieces with a tenderness that suggests they are his children. When I ask if he thinks he might sculpt again, his eyes grow distant. He holds the small stone in his palm and says only, "I don't know if I'm strong enough."
